According to Taiwanese media reports, Nvidia plans to launch an 800VDC power rack compatible with the MGX architecture in the second half of 2026.

The product can be integrated directly into existing AC infrastructure and delivers 800VDC power to compute racks within the same rack row. Since it does not require major retrofitting of existing buildings and power supply systems, it is expected to lower the upgrade threshold for existing AI data centers.

Nvidia also plans to go a step further and introduce a "Row Power Center" for newly built or high density AI factories. This approach feeds power to multiple rack rows through an overhead 800VDC busway, supports up to 2MW per rack row, and is set to enter actual deployment from 2027. Over the longer term, Nvidia intends to adopt a "DC Power Block" that converts grid electricity directly into 800VDC at the facility level, building out a power delivery architecture for AI factories aimed at the next decade.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics Flashes Red on Glass Substrate Customer Evaluation... Investment Pushed Back Too

Samsung Electro-Mechanics' investment schedule for semiconductor glass substrates is slipping. A bottleneck has emerged in the customer's prototype reliability evaluation.

As a result, the timeline for building out the production line at GlaSSEM, the glass core joint venture, has also been pushed back, and the timing of related equipment orders has become murky.

According to multiple industry officials on the 12th, GlaSSEM, the glass core joint venture between Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Dongwoo Fine-Chem, has been unable to give its partners an equipment order schedule. One industry official said, "As recently as the end of July the mood was that orders were imminent, but right now it is hard to predict when they will resume," adding, "The schedule has been postponed several times, so at this point it has become difficult even internally to roughly estimate when orders will be placed."

Samsung Electro-Mechanics had been conveying equipment orders to partners for the GlaSSEM production line since November last year, but the schedule was pushed back at least three times, to December last year, then March, then June this year. After June, guidance on any follow up schedule disappeared altogether.

The industry points to the failure to obtain reliability evaluation certification for the glass substrate prototype from a global communications chip customer. A person familiar with the matter said, "I understand that the investment schedule was halted because Samsung Electro-Mechanics failed to pass the reliability evaluation," and "Since the prototype has to be remade and resubmitted, further delays to the existing schedule are unavoidable." The person added, "Because a new prototype cannot be produced within one or two weeks, whether the line investment happens within this year is also uncertain."

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is currently making glass substrate prototypes at its Sejong campus. To move to initial volume production, the step after pilot production, it is preparing to build a production line at GlaSSEM, the joint venture with Dongwoo Fine-Chem, a subsidiary of Japan's Sumitomo Chemical. Selection of the main process equipment suppliers, covering deposition, etching, laser drilling and inspection, is mostly complete.

Last month, expectations ran high among equipment makers that orders would begin in August. Samsung Electro-Mechanics had planned to start with deposition tools, which carry the longest lead times, bring the main process equipment into Dongwoo Fine-Chem's Pyeongtaek campus and install it by April next year, and complete the initial production line within the second quarter. It is also known to have considered placing orders for long lead time equipment under the Samsung Electro-Mechanics name first and then transferring the contracts to GlaSSEM.

A delay to Samsung Electro-Mechanics' glass substrate mass production timeline has likewise become unavoidable. Even if orders are placed within this year, factoring in equipment build times, the production line would be ready in the second half of next year at the earliest. The start of mass production is understood to have been pushed out to 2028 or later.

When GlaSSEM was established early last month, Samsung Electro-Mechanics presented a target of operations starting in the second half of 2027. At the recent second quarter earnings announcement, less than a month later, it revised the start of operations to 2028.

Exclusive: SK hynix to Increase NAND Production in China by 50%

SK hynix is resuming construction of its second NAND flash plant in Dalian, China, expanding its local production capacity by approximately 50%. Construction of the Dalian Fab 2 began four years ago but was suspended for an extended period following the memory market downturn. SK hynix plans to begin installing semiconductor production equipment by year-end and bring the fab into full operation in the first half of next year.

According to semiconductor industry sources on August 11, Solidigm, the NAND subsidiary of SK hynix, resumed investment in Dalian Fab 2 in the first half of this year and restarted construction. Production equipment is expected to begin moving in as early as November, with the fab slated to establish a mass-production system and begin manufacturing NAND flash in the first half of next year. The new line is reportedly designed for monthly wafer input capacity of around 50,000 wafers. Combined with the existing Dalian Fab 1’s capacity of 100,000 wafers per month, this would increase SK hynix’s local production capacity by approximately 50%.

Investment in Dalian is moving forward again after a four-year hiatus as the expansion of artificial intelligence data centers drives a surge in demand for enterprise solid-state drives, pushing NAND prices to nearly 10 times their level a year earlier. SK hynix launched Solidigm after acquiring Intel’s NAND business in 2021, taking over Dalian Fab 1 and the surrounding site before beginning construction of Fab 2 in May of the following year. However, the memory downturn and U.S. restrictions on exports of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China brought progress to a halt, leaving only the fab’s structural framework completed.

With the construction of Dalian Fab 2, SK hynix is pursuing a two-track NAND production and sales strategy. The company plans to manufacture lower-layer NAND based on mature technology in Dalian while concentrating production of advanced, high-layer-count NAND in Cheongju. Dalian is expected to focus on improving productivity for 100-layer-class NAND based on Intel’s mature floating-gate architecture, while production of NAND with more than 300 layers is expected to be concentrated at domestic facilities such as the M17 fab in Cheongju.

The company previously announced that it would invest KRW 19.1 trillion in the Cheongju M17 fab, with plans to open its first cleanroom by the end of 2028 and manufacture next-generation NAND products there. “Dalian Fab 2 is planned to use the same equipment configuration as Fab 1,” an industry source said. “My understanding is that it will have monthly wafer input capacity of between 40,000 and 60,000 wafers.”

According to Chinese media reports, CXMT’s 17nm DDR5 yield has already exceeded 90%.

CXMT products are currently available in relatively large volumes in the spot market in South China, allowing brands to procure chips based on their specific pricing and specification requirements.

However, major U.S. PC makers have imposed strict policies. Dell reportedly prohibits the use of CXMT chips altogether, while HP permits their use only in products sold in mainland China.

Acer and ASUS are said to be more flexible in their procurement decisions and able to adopt CXMT chips without difficulty.

The two companies mainly use CXMT chips in notebook models sold in mainland China and emerging markets, seeking an optimal balance between price and specifications.

However, the number of models using CXMT chips and the volumes involved remain quite limited, reportedly due to concerns about provoking a backlash from the world’s three largest memory manufacturers.

We need to talk about $LASR's 35% crash and understand how the newest geopolitical war over optical equipment affects the AI photonics trade.

Because @pennycheck makes a strong point. Was yesterday's photonics dump related to this? 

TLDR: $LASR stock is down 35% after a weak guide on uncertain procurement of Chinese optical components.

The CEO attributed it to what appears to be China increasing scrutiny on dual-use products for defense tech. He has no timeline either when they'll be back and wasn't specific about what exactly these products were. 

"The particular commodity that I would highlight would be optics. These are not specialized components. They're materials where China has built out an outsized portion of the overall supply chain over time."

On June 18, 2026 a Chinese precision optics company  disclosed that its chairman had been placed under compulsory measures by Shanghai Customs anti-smuggling. The alleged violation: declaring exported lenses containing germanium as ordinary optical glass to get around export licensing. So suppliers are on edge.

I don't think there's a big read through into datacom optics from this - $LITE, $COHR, $AAOI. In my view, Chinese is getting most aggressive on defense linked optical products. This was already in motion with a Germanium ban, which is needed for IR sensors for drones, and we've seen escalating actions there for months.

$LASR's diodes run around 900nm on gallium arsenide  while lasers from $LITE $COHR $AAOI are Indium phosphide. From my rather limited research, it doesn't appear there's many shared components from $LASR's products with data center optics. InP has already been under Chinese export control since February 2025 and its well documented/understood as a chokepoint.

That being said if there is some kind of Chinese transceiver ban from the U.S. (rumored) we could potentially see tighter InP export controls in return from China if U.S. targets their domestic photonics companies like Innolight and Eptolink, which would have a negative impact.

For now looks to be defense focused but this optical war with China needs to be watched.

存储下一个买盘似乎出现苗头了

存储现在不缺抄底资金，缺的是持续性买盘。

每次三星、海力士、美光大跌，都会有人接。但这些资金很多是短线抄底、空头回补，能拉出一两天反弹，却很难推动一轮稳定行情。

问题还是出在波动率。

现在韩国股市波动率太高，而三星和海力士又占了KOSPI很大权重。机构一旦要降低风险，最直接的做法就是先减掉这些高波动、高弹性、流动性又好的仓位。

所以高波动率对存储有两层影响。

第一，新资金不敢持续买。
第二，已经在场内的资金，也会优先减仓。

这也是为什么存储的基本面可能没变，股价却依然很脆弱。市场一旦进入risk off，资金未必会先卖基本面最差的公司，而是先卖最能降低组合波动率的资产。

相比微软、谷歌、亚马逊这类现金流更稳定的大科技，存储的周期属性更强，对产品价格、供需、库存和CapEx都更敏感。

当市场愿意承担风险时，存储弹性最大。
当市场开始收缩风险时，存储也最容易先被卖。

所以我现在更关注的，不是下一次谁来抄底，而是谁愿意连续买。

真正有效的信号有几个：

1. VKOSPI开始持续下降；
2. 三星和海力士的单日波动明显收窄；
3. 外资不再只是单日巨额流入，而是连续多个交易日净买入；
4. 下一次市场调整时，存储不再成为跌幅最大的方向。

当这些条件出现，说明市场开始重新接受存储的风险，机构也重新获得了配置能力。

所以，存储的下一个买盘，不在下一次暴跌里。

它会出现在韩国市场波动率下降之后，持续性资金重新回来，而且市场下跌时，存储不再被优先卖出的那一刻。

上周五韩国股指收盘，波动率跌至69.67，上一次这么低，是在5月27日，韩国市场的杠杆风险也在进一步下降，空间上可能还不确定，但是已经进入明确的左侧区间
